title: Six students, one year of practice before asking (1.1)
hook: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
tomorrow: Q1: where do creatures come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday: consciousness is Brahman, prajnanam brahma, the great saying that closed the Aitareya. Did you notice the knowing of something ordinary? Today, a new Upanishad, and six people with questions. Day four hundred five.

You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You've waited months. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year. We live in a world of instant answers. Type the question, get the answer, scroll on. The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he says to them. Prashna means question. The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.
screen: `YOUR LIST OF QUESTIONS, READY.` → `COME BACK IN A YEAR.` → `PRASHNA MEANS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The Prashna belongs to the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha, son of Bharadvaja. Satyakama, son of Shibi. Gargya, the grandson of Surya. Kausalya, son of Ashvala. Bhargava, from Vidarbha. And Kabandhi, son of Katya. The text says they were devoted to Brahman, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel in hand, sure he could tell them everything. Pippalada says: stay here one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like. And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers. He promises honesty. Think about what the year does. A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex. A question carried for a year, through practice, through ordinary days, has had time to become real. Some questions answer themselves. Some change shape. And the ones still standing are worth a teacher's time. Notice, too, the three things he asks for. Not cleverness. Not money. Discipline, a steady life, and trust. Over the next five days, each student will ask one question, and you'll hear the answers: where creatures come from, which powers hold up the body, where breath comes from, what's awake in sleep, and what happens to the one who meditates on om.
screen: `SIX STUDENTS, FUEL IN HAND.` · `STAY ONE MORE YEAR.` · `IF WE KNOW, WE'LL TELL YOU.` · `A QUESTION CARRIED BECOMES REAL.` · then, large: `EARN THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one question. Sit, and let a question come up that you've been carrying for a while: about your life, a person, what any of this is for. Don't answer it. Just ask it again, slowly, and notice its shape. Is it the same question it was a year ago? Has it grown, or shrunk, or changed into another one? Hold it the way Pippalada's students held their fuel: ready, patient, not in a hurry. The bell holds the time.
Six students. The seekers of the Prashna Upanishad, told by the sage Pippalada to live a year in discipline and faith before asking, and promised only: if we know, we'll tell you.
Your line: earn the question. Today, before you search for the answer to something, carry the question a little longer, and see if it changes. Day four hundred five.

screen: `DAY 405 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?`

howItsDone: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; many Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

original.note: Sanskrit praśna, question: the Prashna Upanishad is built from six students' six questions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good teacher answers right away.
what it means: Pippalada asks his students to practice for a year first, and promises only honesty.
what a scholar hears: yadi vijñāsyāmaḥ, sarvaṃ ha vo vakṣyāma iti, 'if we know, we shall tell you all' (Prashna 1.2). the Upanishad belongs to the Atharva Veda.
